content: Rhinosinusitis refers to the inflammation of the nasal mucosa and paranasal sinuses. The terms sinusitis and rhinosinusitis are often used interchangeably, but rhinosinusitis is preferred because inflammation of the paranasal sinuses rarely occurs without concurrent inflammation of the nasal mucosa. The primary cause of rhinosinusitis is infectious in nature, although it can also be associated with other medical conditions such as allergies. Diagnosis is predominantly clinical, and imaging or other diagnostic studies are generally not required for confirmation. There are no known life-threatening causes of sinusitis. However, certain symptoms warrant attention, such as purulent rhinorrhea lasting 3–4 days, worsening symptoms, or the recurrence of symptoms after initial improvement. New or recurrent fever, increased nasal discharge, or worsening cough may also indicate complications. The diagnosis of sinusitis, as per the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery guidelines, is based on the presence of at least two major symptoms or one major symptom along with two or more minor symptoms. Major symptoms include purulent nasal discharge, nasal obstruction, facial pain, hyposmia or anosmia, and fever. Minor symptoms include headache, cough, halitosis, fatigue, otalgia, and dental pain. When taking a patient’s history, it is important to inquire about exposure to toxins, contaminated water, solvents, or occupational hazards such as work in oil refineries, leather tanning, or textiles. Additionally, ask about prior upper respiratory infections, tobacco use, anatomical abnormalities, acid reflux disease, and the patient’s immunologic status. During the physical examination, look for purulent nasal discharge, nasal speech (rhinolalia), edema, periorbital erythema, and tenderness or pain upon palpation or percussion of the frontal and maxillary regions. Be vigilant for signs of orbital pain, visual disturbances, facial erythema, or meningitis, as these patients require urgent referral to the emergency department. Avoid inappropriate use of antibiotics in acute presentations, as the majority of these infections are viral in origin. Refrain from ordering imaging studies when the diagnosis is clinically evident. Additionally, avoid unnecessary use of decongestants, antihistamines, or topical steroid sprays unless specifically indicated.
